Can Machine Learning Predict Hospital Mortality in Intensive Care Patients?

I explored 15,664 intensive care records to understand how clinical characteristics relate to patient outcomes, then compared machine learning methods to predict the probability of in hospital mortality. This dashboard brings together the analysis, modelling approach and results from my university research project.

01 · Research overview

Why predict hospital mortality?

Intensive care units treat patients with different medical histories, physiological conditions and levels of risk. Understanding how these measurements relate to hospital outcomes is an important research question.

I used a preprocessed extract of the MIMIC III critical care dataset to compare models trained on demographic information, vital signs, admission details and diagnosis records. The outcome was whether a patient died during their hospital stay.

Why class imbalance matters: Almost nine in ten records were survivors. A model that simply predicted survival would appear accurate without effectively identifying patients who died. That is why I focused on ROC AUC when comparing models.

02 · EXPLORATORY DATA ANALYSIS

What did the patient data reveal?

I compared clinical measurements, admission categories and diagnosis information to identify patterns associated with mortality.

Patients who died tended to have lower oxygen saturation and systolic blood pressure, together with higher respiratory rates. These are observed group differences, not causal effects.
Emergency admissions had a 12.5% observed mortality rate, compared with 6.8% for urgent and 3.2% for elective admissions.
The infectious disease grouping had the highest observed mortality in this summary. The groups are broad primary diagnosis categories and should not be interpreted as individual diagnoses.

What stood out?

Vital signs

Oxygen saturation, respiratory rate and blood pressure showed differences across the two patient outcome groups.

Admission circumstances

Observed mortality was greater among emergency admissions than among urgent or elective admissions.

Diagnosis information

Primary diagnosis groups provided another way to explore mortality patterns beyond physiological measurements.

The charts above are generated from the original training records. They describe observed relationships and are not model feature importance rankings.

03 · DATA PREPARATION AND MODEL DEVELOPMENT

From clinical records to model ready data

Preparing the dataset was essential because the models needed consistent numerical predictors and meaningful clinical information.

01 · CleanStandardise diagnosis text, inspect missing values and process dates
02 · EngineerCreate age, diagnosis counts, shock index and oxygenation risk variables
03 · EncodeTurn categorical values and clinical codes into model features
04 · PrepareRemove identifiers and scale features where required
05 · EvaluateCompare training and unseen validation ROC AUC
Feature engineering used medical diagnosis information and vital signs to create additional predictors. The workflow also excluded nonpredictive patient and stay identifiers.

Statistical baseline

Logistic Regression and Regularised Logistic Regression established an interpretable comparison point.

Linear classification

Neighbour and tree methods

kNN, Decision Trees, Random Forest and Extremely Randomised Trees captured different relationships in the data.

Similarity and ensembles

Advanced approaches

Gradient Boosting, XGBoost and Neural Networks were tested for their ability to learn more complex patterns.

Nonlinear prediction
04 · MODEL EVALUATION

Which models worked best?

Explore the recorded results from the final university report. Use the controls to compare training, validation and Kaggle ROC AUC without retraining the models.

Interactive performance comparison

ROC AUC evaluates how well a model ranks patients by outcome. A value of 1 is perfect discrimination; 0.5 is equivalent to chance ranking.
Several models fitted the training set almost perfectly but performed less well on validation data.
The Decision Tree, kNN and Neural Network models had notably larger training to validation gaps than Logistic Regression or XGBoost.

05 · FINDINGS AND REFLECTION

What did the research show?

The final outcome was not only a strong model score, but a clearer understanding of how clinical data and modelling choices affect prediction quality.

01 · Clinical measurements matter

Differences in physiological measurements, admission circumstances and diagnosis groups supported the use of clinical information for mortality prediction.

02 · Data preparation is essential

Cleaning records and engineering clinically informed features helped convert raw patient information into useful predictors for the models.

03 · Test performance matters most

Perfect training scores did not guarantee strong results on unseen data. XGBoost achieved the highest reported validation ROC AUC.

My research conclusion

This project gave me practical experience using R to explore healthcare data, develop predictive features, compare machine learning methods and interpret model performance. XGBoost achieved the strongest validation result, while regularised Logistic Regression remained a competitive and more interpretable alternative.

The most valuable lesson was the importance of comparing approaches carefully, recognising overfitting and looking beyond a single performance metric.

Limitations and responsible interpretation

The MIMIC III records come from historical intensive care admissions at one hospital. These findings should not be assumed to generalise to every patient population or healthcare setting. ROC AUC measures ranking performance, not the calibration of predicted risks or suitability for clinical decisions.

External validation, calibration analysis and clinical assessment would be necessary before considering real world use.
